AGAINST THOSE WHO ATTACK THE PEOPLE WHO URGE OTHERS TO TAKE UP THE MONASTIC LIFE [?] [44]

1. After their long captivity, the children of the Hebrews came home and wanted to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, which had lain in ruins for many years. Then certain barbarous and savage men set out to stop them. These men had no reverence for God, to whom the temple was being raised. They felt no pity for the misfortune of the people, from which they had only recovered at last and with great difficulty. Nor did they fear the punishment that God sends on those who dare such things. At first they tried to stop the building on their own. When they got nowhere, they sent letters to their king, calling that city rebellious, seditious and warlike, and they persuaded him to let them halt the building. With this authority from him, they attacked the builders with a large force of horsemen and stopped the work for a time. They were very proud of this victory, though they should have been mourning over it, and they thought their plot had succeeded. But this was only the prelude and the beginning of the evils that were very soon to overtake them. For the work was finished and brought to a splendid completion. And they learned, and through them everyone else learned, that they had not been fighting against men after all. Neither Mithredath then, nor anyone else who chooses to fight men set on doing some good, is fighting those men. He is fighting God himself, who is honored through them, before he is fighting them. And whoever fights against God can never come to a good end. At the start of his daring such a person may suffer nothing terrible. If he does escape suffering, it is because God is calling him to repentance and giving him a chance to come to his senses, as if from drunkenness. But if he goes on in his drunken violence and gains nothing from such great forbearance, he will at least do others the greatest good: his punishment will teach them never to take up battle against God, since no one can escape that invincible hand. Such misfortunes did in fact overtake those men at once, and the scale of that tragedy made all other misfortunes look small. [45] For after the slaughter and the countless … [Editorial note, garbled: … a little later two manuscripts read: … the greatest things from the … [?] and Savile in the margin: by the magnitude of the tragedy …]

… For what reason, and with what goal, do they throw stones at the sky, hurl darts at heaven, and make war on the God of peace? Shimshai, the Apharsathchites, the rulers of the Assyrians and all those others were barbarians, as you can see from their very names. They were far removed from the Jewish way of life, [46] and they did not want to see the people living next to them grow strong, because they thought that the power of those people would then overshadow their own authority. But these people of ours: what freedom did they lose, what security was cut away from them, which of the rulers did they have on their side, that they dared to do these things? The others had the kings of the Persians wanting the same things they wanted. Our rulers, I am convinced, desire and pray for the very opposite. That is why I am so perplexed: while our emperors live in piety, you tell me that such things are being dared in the middle of our cities.

He replied: What if you learn something even more astonishing than this? The people who do these things want to be thought pious and call themselves Christians, and many of them are even among the baptized. One of them, filled with the devil's breath, dared to say with that foul tongue of his that he would abandon the faith and sacrifice to demons. He was choking with rage at the sight of free and well-born men, who could have lived in luxury, being led into this harsh life.

When I heard this, I was struck by an even harder blow. I pictured all the evils that would come of it and lamented over the whole world, and I said to God: “Take my soul from me, lead me out of my distresses, release me from this perishable life, and bring me to that place where no one will say such things and I will not hear them. I know that when I leave this world the outer darkness will receive me, where there is much weeping and gnashing of teeth. Still, I would rather hear teeth gnashing than hear words like these.”

When he saw how bitterly I was grieving, he said: “This is not the time for that. You will never win back those who have perished, or are perishing, by these tears, and I do not think the evil will stop. We must find a way to put out the fire and stop the plague, as far as it lies with us. If you will listen to me, leave off these lamentations and write a discourse of exhortation to those who are sick and rebellious, for their own salvation and for the common salvation of all people. I will take the book and put it into the hands of the sick in place of any other medicine. I have many friends who suffer from this sickness, and they will agree to read it through once, twice, many times, and I know they will soon be free of the plague.”

“You,” I said, “are measuring my ability by the measure of your love. I have no power with words, and I am ashamed to use what little I seem to have on such a subject. I am ashamed before no one so much as before all the Greeks, both those living now and those still to come, whom always no less than for the doctrines …

[Editorial notes, garbled: … Apharsathchites and the rulers. These names are corrupt [?]. ‘What freedom of hers’ is a faulty reading. [?] ‘planning the same things.’ [?] And one manuscript: ‘bringing [it] to the sick, I will put.’ Morel, however, and … One manuscript has ‘sufficiently.’ ‘Entirely.’ [?]]

… to receive some help from the very God they are fighting, for the healing of those who fight him. [48] And he will surely give it, because he loves humankind and does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live.

So I sent him away and set to work on this discourse. Suppose this were the only evil: that those holy and wonderful men of God are dragged off and torn about, hauled into the courts, beaten, and made to suffer everything else I have just described. If none of the harm fell back on the heads of those who dare such things, I would be so far from grieving over what is happening that I would have laughed at them, long and heartily. When little children hit their mothers and there is no danger in it, they make the mothers they are hitting laugh a great deal. The angrier the child is, the more the mother is delighted, until she melts and doubles over with laughter. But suppose the child hits her again and again and violently, and at some point hurts himself: on a needle pinned into his mother's tunic at the girdle, perhaps, or on the weaving shuttle at her breast, which catches his hand. Then, at that very moment, the mother stops laughing and is seized by greater anguish than the child who was hurt. For the moment she tends the wound, but afterward she forbids him, with stern threats, ever to do such things again, so that he will not be hurt the same way again.

We would do the same, then, if we saw that this childish rage, these blows of infants, brought them no great ruin. But a little later, even if they do not notice it now while their rage holds them, they will weep and wail and lament. It will not be the crying of little children. It will be the crying in the outer darkness, in the unquenchable fire. So let us do as the mothers do, but with this one difference: we will discuss these things with the children not with threats and insults, as the mothers do, but with much coaxing and gentleness. As for the saints, they suffer no harm from any of this; they gain a greater reward and greater confidence before God. If we speak of the good things to come, you may well laugh out loud, since you are always practicing that kind of laughter. But present facts you will not disbelieve, however fond of laughter you may be. You could not disbelieve them even if you wanted to, because the facts themselves speak out against you.

You have surely heard of Nero. The man became notorious for his licentiousness: he was the first and only person in such a position of power to invent new kinds of debauchery and indecency. This Nero brought against blessed Paul, who happened to live at the same time, the same kind of charges that you bring against these holy men. Paul had persuaded a concubine of Nero's, a woman he loved passionately, to accept the word of faith, and at the same time he persuaded her to free herself from that impure relationship. Bringing these charges, then, and calling Paul a corrupter and a deceiver and all the other names you use, [49] Nero first put him in chains. When he could not persuade him to give up advising the girl, he finally had him killed. What harm did this do to the one who suffered evil? What good did it do to the one who did evil? What benefit did the man who was killed then not …

[Editorial notes: One manuscript has ‘was becoming.’ The same manuscripts: ‘of the fine leaps’ [?]. Others: ‘of many.’]

… and their eyes were fixed on the sight. She said: “This is my own true child, and the deed is mine. Eat, for I have eaten too. Do not be softer than a woman or more tender-hearted than a mother. But if you are pious and turn away from my sacrifice, well, I have eaten half, so let the rest be left for me too.” After this they went out trembling. This was the one thing that made them afraid, and this was the only food they left to the mother. At once the whole city was filled with the horror of it. Each person pictured the deed before his eyes and shuddered as if he had done it himself. The starving were eager to die, and those who had died first were called blessed, since they had not lived to hear and see such evils. The horror was quickly reported to the Romans as well. Some of them refused to believe it, others pitied the people, but most were driven to an even fiercer hatred of the nation.

6. The Jews suffered these things, and much worse, not only because they crucified Christ but because afterward they also hindered the apostles from speaking the message of our salvation. That is why blessed Paul accused them of this and foretold these evils for them, saying: “Wrath has come upon them to the uttermost.”

“And what has this to do with us?” he says. “We are not leading anyone away from the faith or from the preaching.”

And what is the use of faith, tell me, without a pure life? But perhaps you do not know this either, since you have never listened to any of our teachings. I will list for you Christ's own sentences. Watch whether a person's life is never called to account on that day, and whether punishments are decreed only for faith and doctrine. When he went up the mountain and saw a great crowd streaming around him, after his other exhortations he said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father.” And: “On that day many will say to me, ‘Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you.’” [55] And he said that the one who hears his words but does not do them is like a foolish man who builds his house on the sand and makes it an easy prey for rivers and rains and winds. In another place, speaking to the people, he says: “As fishermen, when they haul in the net, throw out the bad fish, so it will be on that day, when the angels cast all who have sinned into the furnace.” Speaking about licentious and impure people, he said: “They will go away to where the undying worm is and the unquenchable fire.” And again: “A king made a wedding feast for his son, and seeing a man dressed in filthy clothes, he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ And the man was speechless. Then he said to the servants …”

[Editorial notes, garbled: Others: ‘and beside the.’ [?] One: ‘I therefore have eaten.’ ‘And scarcely this.’ [?] … edition of Josephus, ‘as though it had been newly done by him’ [?] … ‘eagerness of the starving’ [?]. Two manuscripts: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not in your name.’ So Savile, corrected. Morel [?]. So Savile and two manuscripts; Morel reads ‘worse.’]

… leading the soul once betrothed to God away from fellowship with him, handing it over to the impure, and forcing it to lie with them [?] … If those who find it are few, far fewer are those who [reach] the end [?] … shamefully and insolently [?] … able to reach it first [?]. For not all who set foot on [the road] of virtue were able to stand at its end [?] … but some [fell] at the beginning and others in the middle. Stripping off the garments of virtue, they put on the garments of the passions instead, filthy, torn and foul-smelling, … [?] and making it look … [?]. Filled with all their own impurity, they never stop parading their insults against it. For [?] of this foul and lawless … [?] like drunkards, who burn all the hotter once they have filled themselves with drink, so these men too leap on it all the more [?] the more they abuse it. They stab it from every side and bite it and pour their own venom into it, and they do not stop until they have brought it into their own condition, or until it has been given back [?] from the body.

What tyranny, what captivity, what devastation, what enslavement, what war, what shipwreck, what famine [can compare with] these? Who is so senseless, inhuman, unfeeling and callous that he would not want, as far as it lies with him, to free a soul so insulted and abused from that madness and outrage, but would stand by and watch it suffer such things? And if that is the mark of a harsh and stony soul, where, tell me, shall we place these people? They are not content to look on. They do a far greater evil. There are men eager to leap into the midst of the dangers, who do not shrink from thrusting their hands down the very throat of the beast, who even endure the stench and the dangers in order to pull out souls already swallowed, from the demon's own gullet. These people not only refuse to praise or welcome such men; [55] they drive them out on every side and make war on them.

8. “What then?” he says. “Have all who live in the cities perished? Are they all storm-tossed? Must we leave the cities and turn them into wastelands, move to the desert and live on the mountaintops? Is this what you command and legislate?”

Far from it! On the contrary, as I said before, I wished and I still pray that we might enjoy such peace, and that the tyranny of these evils might be so completely overthrown, that not only would those in the cities have no need to take to the mountains, but those who live in the deserts, like exiles, might after a long time come back to their own city. But what am I to do? I am afraid that in my eagerness to give them back to their homeland I may instead hand them over to evil demons. Wanting to free them from the desert and from exile, I may make them fall away from all philosophy and tranquility. And if you think you can shame and frighten me by pointing to the multitude of people in the city, as though I could not bring myself to condemn the whole world, I will take up Christ's sentence and stand with it against this objection of yours. For you will not dare a thing so full of presumption as to set yourself against the verdict of the one who is then to …

[Editorial notes, garbled: … and two manuscripts [?]: ‘the souls fitted to God.’ Morel: ‘forcing them.’ [?] Morel: ‘putting on passions’; but ‘passions’ is missing in the manuscripts. Below [?] in the text and Morel: ‘filling up with their own’; Savile in the margin: ‘smearing over besides’; two manuscripts: ‘using up besides.’ Savile: ‘For you could not bear to endure a thing so full of daring’; two manuscripts likewise ‘to endure … of daring.’ Morel [?] in the text.]

… for, to pass over the rest, the very thing that forced us to take up this discourse: is it not enough by itself to show how wicked the prevailing disease is? If the furthest limit of wickedness is to sin without feeling it, without even noticing one's own sins, where shall we rank these new lawgivers of this novel and utterly absurd legislation? They drive away the teachers of virtue with all the more boldness, when they ought to be defending those who dare to raise their voices for virtue.

[Editorial note: For ‘they would taste’ it seems one should read ‘they would not taste.’]

[57] TO AN UNBELIEVING FATHER: SECOND DISCOURSE

1. These things alone are enough to cause amazement and horror. If anyone should now apply to them that prophetic saying, “Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly,” and, “Astonishing and horrible things have happened in the land,” every such word would be fitting. But what is worse is this: it is not only strangers, people who have no connection with those being counseled, who are indignant and annoyed at such things. Relatives and fathers have learned to be angry over them too.

I am well aware that many are not very surprised when fathers do this. What makes them choke with rage, they say, is seeing people who are not fathers, friends or relatives, who have no other connection at all, and who are often complete strangers to those who choose the life of philosophy, react in exactly this way. These people are stung more sharply than the fathers, and they make war on those who persuaded the young men and accuse them. To me it is the opposite that seems astonishing. For people who have no claim of either family ties or friendship, it is not surprising that they should be pained at good things that belong to others. Sometimes they are gripped by envy. Sometimes they think that other people's ruin is good fortune for their own wickedness. It is a wretched and miserable way to think, but they think it all the same. But consider the parents: they gave their children life and raised them, they pray every day to see their children more honored than themselves, and they do and suffer everything for this purpose. That these very people should suddenly change, as if seized by drunkenness, and be pained when their children are led to philosophy: this is what amazes me most of all, and I say it is proof enough that everything has been corrupted.

No one could say that this happened even in earlier times, when error reigned openly. It did happen once in a Greek city, but that city was under a tyranny. Even then it was not one of the parents, as it is now. It was the men who had seized the acropolis. Or rather, not all of them: the most abominable among them summoned Socrates and ordered him to give up his discourses on philosophy. But that man was a tyrant, an unbeliever and a cruel man. He did everything with a view to overturning the state and reveled in other people's misfortunes, and he knew that nothing could overturn the best of states like such a command. That is why he dared to give it. These men, by contrast, are believers, living in cities that are supposedly well governed, and making decisions about their own children, and yet they dare to say what the [tyrant said] about those under his tyranny [?] … the parent to teach his offspring what is good for him.

[Editorial notes: Two manuscripts: ‘they may lead.’ So Savile and two manuscripts. But Morel: ‘rather to contend.’]

Our contest is against these alone, even though it is the harder one and gives the opponent more holds to grip; for the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit, since they are foolishness to him. It is as if someone tried to make a man long for a kingdom when he is not willing first to be persuaded that the thing exists at all. Yet even with our arguments confined in so narrow a space, I chose to make this contest against these alone. Against the believer we have many just claims, but the sheer excess of shame overshadows the pleasure that comes from having so many. I am ashamed whenever I am forced to argue at length with him about these things, and I fear that this would be the one charge the pagan could justly bring against me. On every other point, by the grace of God, we will easily overcome him, and if he is willing to be fair-minded we will quickly bring him over not only to a love of this way of life, but also to a desire for the very doctrines on which this life is founded. I am so far from fearing the contest with him that I will first make him even more formidable in my argument, and only then come to grips with him.

Let us suppose, then, that this father is not only a pagan, but also richer than all other men, conspicuous, and established in great power. Let him have many fields, many houses and countless talents of gold. Let him come from the most royal of cities and from the most illustrious family. Let him have no other children and no hope of having any in the future, so that all his fortunes ride on this one son. Let the son himself be full of fine prospects, expected soon to rise to the same office, to outshine his father, and to eclipse everyone in worldly affairs. Then, in the midst of these hopes, let someone come and talk to him about this philosophy, and persuade him to laugh at all those things, put on a coarse cloak, leave the city and flee to the mountain, and there plant, water, carry water and do all the other things monks do, which seem cheap and contemptible. Let him also go barefoot and sleep on the ground. Let this handsome young man, who lived in such luxury and honor and had such hopes, become thin and pale, and let him wear clothes cheaper than his own servants'. Have we given the accuser enough holds? Have we built up our opponent sufficiently? If not, we will supply him with still other pretexts. On top of all this, let him set every device in motion to change his son's mind, and all in vain, because the boy stands as if on a rock and rises above the rivers, the rain and the winds. Let such a father lament and shed tears, so as to inflame anger against us all the more, and let him keep accusing us to everyone he meets, saying: "I begot him, I raised him, I toiled through all his years, doing and suffering everything that naturally comes with having children. I had high hopes. I engaged tutors, I called in teachers, I spent money, I often lay awake worrying about his good conduct and his education, so that he would fall short of none of his ancestors and outshine them all. I expected him to support me in my old age. As time went on I was making plans about a wife and marriage, about office and power. But suddenly, like a thunderbolt or a hurricane falling from somewhere, [?]"

Where, then, shall we begin our answer to him? With wealth and money, since that is what he laments most of all, and everyone thinks it most terrible when rich children are drawn into this life. Tell me, then: whom do we all call blessed and enviable? Is it the man who is always thirsty, who needs another cup before he has drained the first, and who stays in this state forever? Or is it the man who stands above that necessity, who is never thirsty and never dragged down into needing this drink? Is not the first like a man with a fever, under the most grievous compulsion even if he can draw water from springs? And is not the second free with true freedom and healthy with true health, and has he not risen above human nature?

Again, suppose a man in love with a woman lies with her continually, yet after each union burns for her all the more, while another stands outside this madness and is not caught by the evil even in a dream. Which of them do we count enviable and blessed? Is it not the second? And who is wretched and miserable? Is it not the one sick with that empty passion, which can never be quenched and is only inflamed by the remedies devised for it? And if, on top of all this, he were to congratulate himself on his sickness, refuse to be freed from that compulsion, and lament those who have been freed from the passion, as this father now does, would he not be all the more pitiable and wretched? He is not only sick; he does not even know that he is sick, and so he neither wishes to be freed nor stops mourning those who have been.

Let us apply this argument to the getting of money, and we shall see who is wretched and miserable. This passion is more violent and more frenzied than those others, so it can cause more pain. Its flame is fiercer, and it is also more unyielding and stubborn than those others against any consolation devised for it. Those who love drink and bodies reach satiety after enjoyment sooner than those mad for wealth. That is why we had to invent those other cases for the argument, since they are not often seen in actual experience; but of this disease we can supply many examples from real life. Is this why, tell me, you mourn your son: because he has been freed from madness and from such helplessness, because he is not in love with an incurable love, because he stands outside this war and battle?

"But he would not have suffered this," he says. "He would not have longed for more; the enjoyment of what he had would have been enough for him." What you are saying is, one might almost say, contrary to nature. Still, let this too be granted for the sake of argument: suppose he would not have wished to add to what he had, nor been caught by that desire. Even so, I will show that he now lives in greater ease and pleasure. For which is lighter: to worry about so many things, to be bound to such guardianship and slavery, and to fear losing some part of one's property, or to be freed from these bonds as well? Grant that he does not desire further burdens. It is far better to despise even those already laid on him. For if not needing more is agreed to be the greatest good, then to be beyond the need even of what one already has is [?] of a greater [?]

"…and Cebes too, and many others. So, as I said, do not let fear of these things make you give up on saving yourself, and do not be troubled by what you said in court, that if you went away you would not know what to do with yourself. In many places, wherever you go, they will welcome you. And if you wish to go to Thessaly, I have friends there who will value you highly and keep you safe, so that you will lack nothing in Thessaly." What could be sweeter than such abundance?

But that is speaking to a worldly man. If we want to examine the son's wealth more philosophically, you perhaps will not follow the argument, but I must speak for the sake of the judges. So great is the wealth of virtue, so much sweeter and more desirable than the wealth you value, that those who have it would never be willing to take the whole earth in exchange for it, even if the earth turned to gold along with the mountains, the sea and the rivers. If that could happen, you would learn from experience itself that these are not boastful words: having found things far more numerous and greater, they would despise that gold and never trade this wealth for it. And why do I say trade? They would not even choose to take it in addition to their own. Yet if anyone offered you the wealth of virtue together with money, you would receive it with open hands, and so you admit that it is something great and wonderful. These men would not choose your wealth even in addition to their own, so well do they know that it is a contemptible thing.

This too I will make clear from your own examples. How much money do you think Alexander would have given Diogenes, if Diogenes had been willing to accept it? But he was not willing, while Alexander strove and did everything he could to attain Diogenes' wealth one day.

5. Would you like to see your poverty and your son's wealth from another angle as well? Then go and take away his cloak, the only one he has; drive him out of his hut and pull down his dwelling. Even so you will not see him vexed or grieved. He will even thank you for it, because you are pushing him further toward philosophy. But if someone takes just ten drachmas from you, you will never stop weeping and wailing. Who, then, is rich: the one stung by small things, or the one who despises everything there is? And do not stop there; drive him out of the whole country as well, and you will see him laughing at it as at a child at play. But if someone merely drives you out of your homeland, you will think you are suffering the most terrible fate and will not be able to bear the misfortune. He, as though the whole earth and sea belonged to him, will move from one place to another as easily and painlessly as you walk through your own fields, or rather more easily. Even if you can walk through your own land, you must also pass through other people's; he will travel through his own land wherever he goes. Lakes, rivers and springs everywhere give him drink in abundance; his food is vegetables and herbs, and bread from many places. I am not yet telling you that he despises the whole earth as well, [?] a city [?]

…here. Comparing the palace with the wilderness, and the hopes there with the hopes here, you think your son has fallen from heaven itself. So we must first learn that the wilderness does not make a man dishonored, nor does the palace make him brilliant and illustrious. Before coming to reasoned argument, I will free you of this suspicion with examples, not ours but yours.

You have perhaps heard of Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, and also of Plato, the son of Ariston. Tell me, then: which of them became more illustrious? Which is celebrated and on the lips of the many? Is it not the philosopher rather than the tyrant? Yet the one ruled all Sicily, lived in luxury, and spent his life surrounded by great wealth, bodyguards and every other kind of pomp, while the other spent his time in the garden of the Academy, watering and planting and eating olives, setting a cheap table, and far removed from all that pomp. And that is not yet the remarkable part. Even when he became a slave and was sold at the tyrant's will, he was so far from looking more dishonorable than the tyrant on that account that he appeared venerable even to the tyrant himself. Such is virtue: through what it suffers as well as through what it does, it lets neither itself nor those who wrong it stay hidden and unnoticed.

And what of his teacher Socrates? How much more illustrious was he than Archelaus? Yet the one was a king and lived in great wealth, while the other spent his time in the Lyceum and owned nothing but a single cloak, which he was seen wearing winter and summer and in every season of the year. He went barefoot all his life, endured fasting all day long, and ate only bread, which was both his relish and his food. He did not even provide this table from his own house but received it from others, so extreme was the poverty he lived with. And he was so much more illustrious than the king that, though the king often invited him, he would not leave the Lyceum and go to the king's wealth. This is also evident from the fame that prevails today [?]: the philosophers' names are known to many, the kings' to no one.

Then there was the man from Sinope, another philosopher, who was so much richer than these and countless other such kings, and that while living in rags, that when Philip's son, the Macedonian, was leading an army against the Persians, he left everything as soon as he saw him, went to him, and asked him in person whether he needed anything and whether he had any request to make. But he asked for nothing.

Are these examples enough for you, or would you like us to mention others? These men became more illustrious not only than those who shone in palaces but than the ruler himself. They chose a private and untroubled life and did not want to come anywhere near public affairs. And even in public life you will find that the illustrious are not those who live in wealth, luxury and abundance, but those who live in poverty, in simplicity, in an unpretentious life. Among the Athenians there was Aristides, whom the city buried even when he died, and [?] in wealth and birth and luxury and power of speech and strength of body and nobility and the other [?]

…let us examine this. What do you say is the proof of the greatest power? Is it not being able to punish those who harm us and to repay those who do us good? Yet one would not find this power in full even in a king. He has many who harm him whom he cannot harm in return, and many who do him good whom he cannot easily repay. In wars he has often wished to punish enemies who hurt him and did him countless evils, but could not. And friends who performed great feats there he could not repay as they deserved, because they were snatched away before he could reward them and fell in the war itself. What, then, if we show that your son has another power, far greater than this one, which not even kings enjoy, as the argument has shown?

And let no one suppose that we are speaking of the good things in heaven, which you do not believe. We have not forgotten our promises so easily; we will supply the proof from what happens here. If the greatest power is the ability to punish those who harm us, far greater than this is to find a way of life in which no one will be able to harm us even if he wants to. That this is greater than that will become plain and clear if we turn the argument to another example. Tell me, which is better: to be so skilled in war that no one who wounds us escapes unwounded, or to have a body that no one can strike, even if he tries countless times? Surely everyone sees that the second is both more powerful and more godlike than the first. And not only this, but there is something far higher still. What is that? To know remedies that make every wound disappear. There are, then, three ways: first, being able to punish wrongdoers; second, a higher one, being able also to heal one's own wounds (for this does not necessarily follow from the first); and third, being vulnerable to no human being at all, which is indeed beyond human nature. This last, we will show, is what your son has.

6. To show that these words are not empty noise: while searching, we have found along the way yet another power, greater than even this great one. One will see people not only unable but even unwilling to harm such men, so their security is doubled. What could be more godlike than this life, in which no one will either want to do him harm or be able to if he wants? This is especially true when the unwillingness does not arise from inability, as it does with many people, but from finding no reason to harm him. If inability were all there was, it would be nothing so great, for much hatred would arise in those who want to do wrong but cannot. Even so, that too is no small kind of blessedness.

Let us examine this first, if you like. Tell me, who will ever want to harm a man who has nothing in common with other people: no contracts, no land, no money, no business, nothing else at all? Over what land will anyone quarrel with him? Over what slaves? Over what glory? What would anyone fear from him? What would sting anyone into it? We are moved to harm others by envy, or fear, or anger. But this most royal of men stands above all of these. For who will envy the [?]

…[?] thought to be [?] than his own. For just as in matters of money, when something must be spent, people listen to them rather, so too they ask them to take up their cause [?].

8. If you like, let him accomplish nothing through others, only through himself. Let us bring someone who has suffered misfortune both to him and to you, or rather not to you but to the king himself, and then see who will be better able to take care of him. And let the first one brought be the man who has suffered the most terrible thing of all. Suppose a man has an only son and loses him in the bloom of youth. Neither magistrate nor king nor anyone else will be able to help him, let alone you, for you can give him nothing like what he has lost. But if you bring him to your son, your son will first quickly lift him up by his mere appearance, his dress and his dwelling, and persuade him to count human things as nothing. Then with words he will easily drive away the cloud. From your house, on the other hand, the man will come away with even more grief. When he sees your house free of trouble, full of prosperity and with an heir, he will burn all the more. From your son, though, he will come away gentler and more philosophical. Seeing your son disregard so much wealth, glory and splendor, he will not grieve so much for the one who died. How can it sting him to have no heir to his property when he sees another man despising all these things? He will also accept the words of philosophy more readily from one who proves them true by his deeds. But if you so much as dare to open your mouth, you will fill him with deep despondency, as someone philosophizing about other people's misfortunes. Your son, teaching him by deeds, will easily persuade him that death is nothing more than sleep. He will not list the many fathers who have suffered the same thing; he will point to himself, practicing for death every day in the body and always prepared for it. And having made the teaching about the resurrection more credible, he will send the man away relieved of the heavy weight of his grief. Far more than the friends at the funeral meals and memorial feasts, your son's words and the proof of his deeds will be able to comfort the sufferer. That is how he will heal this man.

If you like, let another man be brought to him, one whose eyes have been destroyed by a long illness. How will you be able to help him? Your son, by showing that this is nothing terrible, shut up as he is in a small cell, hastening toward another light, and counting the present light as nothing compared with that one, will teach him to bear his misfortune nobly. But can you persuade those who are afflicted to bear it like philosophers? Not at all; you will only trouble them more, for we usually see our own misfortunes more sharply amid our neighbors' good fortune. Your son will restore these people too more easily. I pass over the help of his prayers, which is far greater than all of this; I pass over it because my argument is now addressed to you.

And if you want to be honored because of your son and not despised (for it is natural that you should desire this too), I do not know how you could have achieved it better than by having a child who surpasses human nature, who appears so illustrious all over the world, and who, for all this renown, has not a single enemy. For in that position of power [?], many [?]

[?] now more highly esteemed, better provided for and more powerful, and having [?] occasions, you are being wronged [?], not sufficing [?] freer, and more your servant than before, with such greatness of mind: why then, tell me, are you mourning? Because you no longer tremble every day in case he falls in war, or offends the emperor, or is caught by the envy of his fellow soldiers? Don't the fathers of men who are well thought of fear these things, and more besides? People who have set a child on some high place cannot help trembling in case he falls, and it is the same for those who raise their sons to high office. "But the belt, the cloak and the herald's cry bring a certain pleasure." And for how many days, tell me? Thirty, a hundred, twice as many? And what comes after? Doesn't all of that pass away like a dream, like a fable, like a shadow? Now, though, his honour lasts to the end, or rather beyond death, and much more then. No one will take this office from him, because he was elected not by men but by virtue itself. "But I wanted to see him wearing costly clothes, riding on horseback, with a crowd of servants, feeding hangers-on and flatterers." Why did you want this? Wasn't it to give him pleasure through all these things? Then if you hear him say (perhaps you will not believe us) that he thinks this life so much sweeter than the life of those who live in luxury, fornication, music, hangers-on, flatterers and every other kind of softness that he would choose ten thousand deaths many times over rather than leave this pleasure and jump across to that one, what will you say to that? Don't you know how much pleasure there is in a quiet life? Perhaps no one else knows either, since no one has ever yet tasted it in its pure form. And when splendour is added, and these things that do not normally mix come together again, security and good repute, what could be better than this life? "But why do you talk to me about this," he says, "when I stand far from philosophy?" Then why do you stop your son from coming near it? It is enough that the loss stops with you. Don't you think it the greatest loss when you reach extreme old age, having gained nothing good from your youth, and then resent your old age? "But the very reason we resent it," he says, "is that youth did us a great deal of good." What great things? Show me an old man who still holds those great things. If he had them and they had lasted, he would not lament as if stripped of everything. But if they flew away and withered, what great things are they, to be put out so quickly? Your son will not suffer this. If he ever reaches a long old age, you will see him not complaining as you do but rejoicing, glad and exultant, for that is when his goods are at their height. Your wealth, even if it held countless goods, kept them to the first part of life. His wealth is not like that: it remains in old age and goes with him after death. That is why you, seeing your property grow in old age, and many [?] of glory and luxury [?] [Textual note: variant reading προσέρχηται. [?] Savile [?]; but Morel reads "but remains also in old age … you on the one hand many of glory and of luxury," [?] omitting much.]

in tumult, confusion, frenzy and madness, and [?] in great agitation and turmoil. But the pleasure we have is not like that, God forbid! It always keeps the soul free from storms and brings no tumult or agitation. It brings a pure joy, sincere and glorious, a joy without end, far more powerful and intense than yours. Here is the proof that this pleasure is sweeter: fear is enough to drive yours away. If the emperor sends down letters threatening death, most people will fly from that pleasure. But even if someone threatens ten thousand deaths, he will not persuade people to despise this one; he will be laughed at instead. So this pleasure is more powerful than that one and sweeter, and does not even admit of comparison with it. Do not begrudge your child, then, as he crosses over from goods that flow away, or rather do not even exist, to goods that are real and last. Do not mourn someone who deserves to be called blessed. Mourn anyone who is not like him, carried about in the present life as if in the tidal straits of the Euripus. Now for the main point. Even if you are an unbeliever and a pagan, you will still accept this argument. You have surely heard of Cocytus and the fiery rivers of Pyriphlegethon, of the water of the Styx, of a Tartarus as far below the earth as the earth is below heaven, and of many kinds of punishment. The pagans could not speak of these things truly, as they really are, because they were moved by their own reasonings and by things they half-heard from us; still, they grasped some image of the judgement. You will find poets, philosophers and storytellers all philosophizing about these doctrines. You also hear of the Elysian plain, the Islands of the Blessed, meadows and myrtles, a gentle breeze and abundant fragrance, choirs spending their time there clothed in white robes, dancing and singing hymns. In short, you hear of a recompense laid up for both the wicked and the good after they depart from here. How then do you think the good, and those who are not good, live with such thoughts? The wicked turn these things over in their minds, and even if the affairs of the present life go well for them, without pain and with great pleasure, are they not driven along as if by the whip of conscience and the expectation of the terrors that await them? And the good, even if they suffer countless evils, have, as Pindar says, a hope that nurtures youth, which does not let them feel their present evils. So in this respect too that pleasure is greater. It is far better to begin with toils that last only a while and end in endless rest than to taste briefly what seems sweetest and finish in evils more bitter and more crushing. And when it is also agreed that even here this life is sweeter, must we not now do what I said at the beginning, and pity those who weep over such goods? Your son, then, deserves not lamentation but applause [?] [Textual note: The same manuscripts read "but that one." [?] Morel reads δέξεται; [?] δέξαιτο, which we have adopted. [?] codex: "do you think … live with such thoughts." Another: "do you think … live with these thoughts." The passage of Pindar [is found] nowhere [?].]

Come then, let us now also teach the believing father that he must not make war on those who are leading his son towards what pleases God. And yet this argument too is in danger of being superfluous for us, and of turning out the opposite of what I said earlier. Then I said that the law does not compel me to strip for this contest against the pagan: the apostle Paul told us to judge only those inside, and so released us from fighting those outside. Now, it seems, we are not even answerable for these bouts. If it seemed shameful before this to argue these matters with a Christian, it is much more so now. How can the believer not sink with shame at needing to be exhorted about things that not even the unbeliever could argue against? What then? Shall we keep silent for this reason and say nothing? Not at all. If there were someone who would guarantee the future and make it plain to us that no one will ever dare such things again, then we too ought to keep quiet and do the past the kindness of letting it be forgotten. But since we have no trustworthy guarantor of this, exhortation is now necessary. If it finds people sick with this disease, it will do its work. If no one falls into the illness, what we pray for has come about. Physicians too, once they have prepared medicines for the sick, pray that no patient will come to need them. So we too pray that none of our brothers will need this exhortation. But if it does happen, which God forbid, the "second voyage," as the proverb says, will not escape them. So let us now picture the believer as exactly like the unbeliever, resembling him in everything except his belief about God. Let him lament in the same way, roll at everyone's feet, hold up his grey hair, his old age and his bereavement, say all those things, and stir the judges to as much anger as he likes. Or rather, with this man our case is no longer heard before human judges. He has heard what the men among us who were filled with the divine Spirit taught about the dread and fearful tribunal that follows our departure from here. Before everything else we must remind him of that day: of the fire flowing like a river, the flame that is never quenched, the sunlight that vanishes, the moon that is hidden, the stars that fall, the heavens rolled up, the powers shaken, the earth shaken and heaving on every side, the fearful blast of trumpets sounding one after another, the angels running through the whole world, the thousands standing by, the tens of thousands ministering, the armies arriving with the Judge himself, the [?] shining before [?] [Textual note: [?] in one codex [?]. Savile in the text, with two manuscripts, reads "we are answerable"; but in the margin and Morel read "we are free." [?] παρασκευάσαι [?] παρασκευάσασθαι [?]. Soon after, one manuscript reads "about the things of the dread."]

the Only-begotten, wishing to teach that this debt must be paid and that great evils await those unwilling to pay it, said: "Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea." And the man who brought back the talent is punished with that punishment not because he lost anything of his own, but because he neglected the salvation of his neighbours. So even if every part of our life is in perfect order, it does us no good, since this one sin is enough to drown us in the sea of Gehenna. No argument will rescue those who were unwilling to help their neighbour in bodily things; even if they have practised virginity, they will be thrown out of the bridal chamber. Then how could the man who failed in something far greater (for care of the soul is far greater) not deservedly suffer every terror? God made human beings to be useful not only to themselves but to many others. That is why Paul calls the faithful "lights": he shows that they must be useful to others as well. A light that gives light only to itself would not be a light. That is also why he says that those who neglect their neighbours are worse than the pagans, in these words: "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." What do you take "provide" to mean here? Supplying the necessities of life? I think he means care of the soul. But even if you dispute this, my point stands all the more firmly. If he says this about the body, and hands over to such punishment the man who does not supply this daily food, and calls him worse than the pagans, where will the man who neglects the greater and more necessary thing find himself? 3. Come then, let us now reckon up how great our sin is. Climbing step by step, let us show that neglect of children goes beyond all other sins and reaches the very summit of wickedness. The first step of vice, wickedness and cruelty, then, is to neglect one's friends. Or rather, let us start the argument lower down, for somehow this nearly slipped my mind: the former law, given to the Jews, does not allow us to neglect even the beasts of burden of our enemies, whether they have fallen down or gone astray. It commands us to lead the stray back and to help raise up the fallen. So the first step of vice and cruelty, climbing from the bottom, is to pass by the cattle and flocks of our enemies when they are suffering harm. The second, above that, is to neglect our enemies themselves, for the sin is greater by as much as a human being is worth more than a brute beast. The third after this is to despise our brothers, even if they happen to be strangers to us. The fourth is to neglect our relatives. The fifth is when we disregard not only their bodies but their souls as well when they are perishing. The sixth is when we neglect not only our relatives but even our own children as they are being corrupted. The seventh is when we do not even look for others to take care of them. The eighth is when we hinder and prevent those who wish to do this of their own accord. The ninth is when we not only hinder them but make war on them. So if to the first, the second and the [Textual note: Two manuscripts read "the far greater, the care of the soul," through a scribal slip that omitted words because of similar endings. The same manuscripts read "the faithful must be," less correctly. Savile in the text reads "we seek those who will care," in the margin "we consider." Morel reads "we seek those who will care" (with a different spelling). One codex reads "I make those who will care"; another "we consider those who will care."]

God says this was [no] admonition; he condemned it because it had no vehemence or intensity. So even if [?] (for many have often suffered even harsher things [?]) we do provide for our children, but not as much as we ought, this is not provision either [?], just as Eli's admonition was not, and because of this sin. For where [?] untimely [?] come from [?]. Having stated the charge, he adds the punishment with great anger: "I have sworn to the house of Eli," he says, "that the sin of the house of Eli shall never be atoned for by incense or by sacrifices." Do you see how intense the indignation is, and how unpardonable the punishment? He must perish completely, he says, and not he alone or his sons, but his whole house with him, and there will be no remedy to heal this blow. And yet apart from his negligence towards his sons, God had nothing else to charge that old man with at the time. In every other respect he was admirable, and his whole philosophy can be seen not only from other things but also from what happened in this very calamity. First, when he heard all this and saw that he had come to the extreme of punishment, he did not complain or resent it. He did not say any of the things most people would be likely to say: "Am I master of other people's wills? I owe a penalty for my own sins. My sons are of age; they alone deserve to be punished." He neither said nor thought any of this. Like a grateful servant who knows only one thing, how to bear calmly whatever comes from his Master even when it is painful, he spoke these words full of philosophy: "It is the Lord; he will do what is pleasing in his sight." His virtue can be seen not only from this but from elsewhere too. When war overtook the Jews, someone came and reported the disasters of the war and how his sons had been cut down in the battle, shamefully and pitiably. He heard this in silence. But when the man added to this slaughter the capture of the ark by the enemy, then at last the old man, darkened by despair, fell backwards from his seat beside the gate, and his back was broken, for he was old and heavy and held in honour, and he had judged Israel for twenty years. Consider the priest, the old man, the man held in honour, who had led the Hebrew race blamelessly for twenty years and lived in times that did not demand great strictness. None of these things could plead for him. Because he did not take strict care of his sons, he perished terribly and pitiably, and the sin of this neglect, like a great wild wave, overwhelmed all those things and buried all his achievements. If that is so, what punishment will overtake us? We live in times that demand far greater philosophy, we fall short of his virtue, and we not only fail to take charge of our children but plot against and make war on those who wish to do so, treating our offspring worse than any barbarian. The barbarians' cruelty stopped at enslavement, at laying waste the homeland and carrying its people off as slaves, and at evils of the body. You enslave the soul itself; you bind it like a captive and hand it over to wicked demons and [?] and to their passions. When you neither give any spiritual counsel yourselves nor let others do it who wish to, you are doing nothing other than this. And let no one tell me that many [?] more than Eli [?] their own [Textual note: [?] reads "to the extreme punishment"; all the others "to the extreme of punishment." [?] his [?] to endure [?].]

commanding them to lead them by every means to the knowledge of God. To the children themselves he gives many commands about their parents. He honours those who are well disposed towards them and punishes the ungrateful, and in this way too he makes the children dearer to those who begot them. When someone makes us masters of something, the honour lays on us the strongest obligation to take care of it. If nothing else, this alone is enough to shame us: that all his affairs lie in our hands. We could not bear to betray quickly someone who had trusted us so much. And when on top of this he shares our anger, is more indignant than the injured parties themselves, and becomes a severe avenger, he binds us to him much more strongly still. That is what God did. Besides these he added a third bond, the bond of nature, or the first, if you prefer. So that fathers would not disregard his commands when told to bring up their children, he laid on them the compulsion of nature. And so that this bond would not be weakened by the children's insolence and break, he fortified it with punishment, both his own and that of the parents themselves. In this way he made the children strictly subject to their parents and at the same time stirred up the parents' affection for them. He bound us to them strongly and strictly not only in this way but in a fourth way too. He does not only punish children who behave badly towards their parents and welcome them when they are good. He does the very same with fathers: he punishes severely those who neglect their children, and honours and praises those who care for them. That old man, illustrious as he was in every other respect, was punished for this neglect alone. And the patriarch was honoured for this care no less than for anything else. When God spoke of the many great gifts he had promised to give him and stated the reason, this is the reason he gave: "For I knew that Abraham would command his sons and his household after him, and they would keep the ways of the Lord God, doing righteousness and justice." I have said all this so that we may learn that God will not calmly put up with the neglect of those he cares about so much. It is not like him to labour so hard for their salvation and then look the other way when they are despised. He will not look the other way. He will be indignant and very angry, as the facts themselves have shown. That is why blessed Paul constantly exhorts: "Fathers, bring up your children in the discipline and admonition of the Lord." If we are commanded to keep watch over their souls as those who will have to give an account, much more is the father who begot the child, brought him up, and has him living with him all the time. A father cannot take refuge in excuses and pardon for his own sins, and he cannot do so for the sins his children commit either. Blessed Paul made this plain as well. When he laid down what sort of people those who come to rule others must be, he required care of children along with all the other qualities they must have, as if there were no pardon for us if our children are corrupted. And rightly so. If vice belonged to human beings by nature, a person might reasonably take refuge in excuses. But since we become bad by choice [Textual note: [?] "of those … so dear." Soon after, the same manuscripts read "for … salvation" [?]. The same: "to look the other way again at these." [?] Gen. 47 [?].]

[?] …has your son ever heard, or ever realized on his own, that a man who swears an oath, even if he swears truly, cannot help offending God? Or that one who bears a grudge cannot be saved? For “the ways of those who bear grudges,” it says, “lead to death.” Or that God so dishonored the slanderer as to bar him even from reading the divine words? Or that he cast the boastful and insolent man out of heaven and handed him over to the fire of Gehenna? Or that he punished the man who looks with licentious eyes as a full-fledged adulterer? And this sin that comes so readily to everyone, judging one's neighbors and so bringing a harsher punishment on oneself: have you ever urged him to flee it, and have you read him the laws of Christ that deal with these things? Or do you not even know what they are? How then will your son be able to keep these things, when the father who is supposed to teach him does not even know the laws about them? If only this were the whole evil, that you give them no useful counsel, it would not be so bad. As it is, you even push them toward the opposite. When fathers urge their sons to work hard at their studies, you hear nothing from them but words like these: “So-and-so, a lowly man of lowly parents, gained power through eloquence. He has held the highest offices, acquired great wealth, married a rich wife and built a splendid house, and he is feared by all and renowned.” Another says: “So-and-so learned Latin, and now he is a brilliant figure at the palace and runs everything inside it.” One points to one man and another to another, but all of them point to those who are esteemed on earth. No one ever mentions those in heaven even once, and if anyone tries to mention them, he is driven off as someone who would overturn everything.

6. So when you sing these things over them like a spell from the very start, you are teaching them nothing but the foundation of all evils. You implant the two most tyrannical passions: I mean the love of money, and the love that is even more lawless than this, the love of empty and vain glory. Each of these is able to overturn everything even by itself. But when both together fall upon the tender soul of a young man, they are like torrents that have joined together. They destroy everything good, piling up so many thorns, so much sand and so much refuse that they leave the soul barren and fruitless of all those good things. Even the pagan writers would bear witness to us on this. Speaking of one of these passions, and not combined with the other but by itself, one of them called it the citadel of evils and another called it the head of evils. And if by itself it is a citadel and a head, what happens when it takes on the far worse and more powerful one, I mean the mania for glory, and, carried along with it, falls upon the young man's soul, takes root and seizes it in advance? Who will be able to pry this disease out after that, especially when the fathers too do and say everything, not so that these evil plants may be shaken loose but so that they may become firmly fixed? Who then is so foolish as not to despair of the salvation of a child brought up this way? For it would be welcome if a soul trained in the opposite [?]

[?] …ever to conceive anything noble and great. Instead, such a soul is sick and enfeebled, held continually by vice as if by a kind of consumption, and so it must eventually end in Gehenna and in the destruction that awaits there.

7. But suppose you say that this is not so, and that it is possible to achieve all virtue while moving in the midst of the world. If you say this not in jest but in all seriousness, do not hesitate to teach us this new and astonishing lesson. For I do not wish to take on so much trouble for nothing, nor to abstain from so many things in vain. But I cannot learn it, because you do not allow it. By what you say and by what you do, you contradict this verdict and teach the opposite. As if you were deliberately bent on destroying your sons, you bid them do everything that makes salvation impossible for those who do it. Look at it from the beginning. “Woe,” it says, “to those who laugh,” but you give them many occasions for laughter. “Woe to the rich,” but you do everything so that they may make money. “Woe to you when all people speak well of you,” but you have often emptied whole estates to win the acclaim of the crowds. Again, “whoever insults his brother is liable to Gehenna,” but you consider weak and cowardly those who bear the insults of others in silence. Christ commands us to disregard quarrels and lawsuits, but you keep them constantly busy with these evils. He commanded us even to pluck out the eye when it does us harm, but you make your closest friends of anyone who can give money, even if they teach the worst vice. He did not permit a man to put away his wife except for the single cause of fornication, but when there is money to be had, you bid them despise this commandment too. He forbade the oath altogether, but if you see it being kept, you laugh. “He who loves his life,” it says, “will lose it,” but you drive them into this love from every side. “If you do not forgive people their trespasses,” it says, “neither will your heavenly Father forgive you,” but you even reproach them when they are unwilling to take revenge on those who have wronged them, and you hurry to raise them to a position of power so that they can. Christ declared that those who love glory do everything in vain, whether they fast or pray or give alms, but you do everything [?] so that they may obtain it. Why go through it all? What has already been said is enough to prepare countless Gehennas, and not only all of it together but each of these things by itself. Yet you heap them all together, load on them the unbearable burden of sins, and send them off like that into the river of fire. How will they ever be saved, when they carry so much fuel for the fire? And the terrible thing is not only that you counsel the opposite of Christ's commands, but also that you cloak vice in fair names. You call constant devotion to the horse races and the theaters “sophistication,” wealth “freedom,” love of glory “magnanimity,” arrogance “frankness,” prodigality “generosity,” and injustice “courage.” Then, as if this were not enough [?]

[?] …not only [?], but the very laws of nature are being overturned. In the scale of licentiousness, fornication is now a small matter. When one pain is more tyrannical than another, its arrival hides the feeling of the first. In the same way, the excess of this outrage no longer lets the unbearable seem unbearable, I mean licentiousness with women. To be able to escape these nets now seems a thing to be grateful for, and the female sex is in danger of becoming superfluous, since young men are filling all its roles in its place. And that is not yet the worst of it. The worst is that so great a pollution is ventured with complete impunity, and lawlessness has become law. No one fears or trembles any longer. No one is ashamed or blushes; instead they even pride themselves on this joke. Those who are chaste are thought mad, and those who admonish are thought deranged. If the admonishers happen to be weaker, they are beaten to pieces; if they are stronger, they are mocked, laughed at and drenched with countless jibes. There is no help from courts or laws, from tutors or fathers, from attendants or teachers. Some of these they have managed to corrupt with money, and others look only to getting their pay. Of the more decent ones, who care for the salvation of those entrusted to them, some are easily deceived and tricked, and others fear the power of the licentious. A man suspected of aiming at tyranny would more easily come through safely than a man who tried to rescue boys from those abominable men would ever escape their hands. And so, as though in a vast wilderness, males commit shameful acts with males in the middle of our cities. And if some have escaped these snares, they will hardly escape the evil reputation of those who suffer such outrages. First, they are very few, and so they would easily be lost among the multitude of the wicked. Second, those foul and accursed demons themselves have no other way of avenging themselves on those who scorned them, and so they strive to injure them in this way. Since they could not deal a mortal blow or reach the soul itself, they try at least to wound the outward adornment that surrounds them and destroy their whole good name. For this reason I have heard many people wondering how it is that another rain of fire has not been sent down even to this day, and how our city has not yet suffered the fate of Sodom. It deserves a punishment all the harsher, inasmuch as it has not come to its senses even from their calamities. For two thousand years now that land has cried out to the whole world through its very appearance, more clearly than any voice, not to dare any such thing. Yet not only have they not grown more hesitant about this sin; they have grown bolder, as if they were contending with God and striving to show by their deeds that the more he threatens them, the more they will press on with these evils. Why then has nothing of the kind happened? Why are the sins of Sodom ventured, while the sufferings of Sodom do not come? Because another, harsher fire awaits them, and a punishment that has no [?]

[?] …nor do they escape the passions of glory. Most of them are gripped by these very passions, and by those of licentiousness, to an even greater excess. When we want to instill eloquence in our children, we not only remove whatever hinders their education but also supply whatever promotes it. We appoint tutors and teachers, spend money and free them from other business. More insistently than the trainers at the Olympic games, we cry out to them about the poverty that comes from lack of education and the wealth that comes from education. We do and say everything, ourselves and through others, to bring them to the goal set before them, and even so we often fail. Yet do we imagine that good character and the strict discipline of the best way of life will come about of their own accord, and this when so many things stand in the way? What could be worse than this folly? We think the easiest thing deserves so much honor and effort, as if it could never be achieved without them, yet we suppose that what is far more difficult will come to us while we sleep, as if it were something cheap and worthless. For the philosophy of the soul is harder and more laborious than an education in letters, just as acting is harder than speaking and deeds are more toilsome than words.

9. “And what need,” someone says, “do our children have of philosophy and a strict way of life?” This is it; this is what has ruined everything: that something so necessary, which holds our life together, is thought superfluous and incidental. If someone saw his son sick in body, he would not say, “What need does he have of pure and perfect health?” He would go to any lengths so that his son might gain health robust enough that the illness would not return. But when the soul is sick, they say their children need no treatment, and after saying such things they dare to call themselves fathers! “What then?” he says. “Shall we all become philosophers, and the business of life vanish?” It is not living as a philosopher, my good friend, but failing to do so that has ruined and corrupted everything. Tell me, who damages the present order? Those who live moderately and decently, or those who devise new and lawless ways of indulging themselves? Those who are eager to grab everyone's possessions, or those who are content with what they have? Those who keep phalanxes of servants and lead swarms of flatterers about with them, or those who think one servant is enough for them? (I am not yet setting out the highest philosophy, but the kind that many can attain.) Those who are kind and gentle and need no honor from the crowd? Or those who demand that honor from their fellow men more insistently than any debt, and who cause countless calamities because so-and-so did not rise for them, did not greet them first, did not bow down or act like a slave before them? Those who practice being ruled, or those who lust after power and office and are ready to do and suffer anything to get it? Those who claim to be better than everyone and so think they may say and do anything, or those who count themselves among the lowest and so curb the irrational license of the passions? Those who build splendid houses and set out lavish tables, or those who [seek] nothing more [?]

[?] …arming people's tongues no longer against their fellow servants, but now against the very Master who rules over all. For tell me, where does all this talk of fate that we hear everywhere come from? Why do most people ascribe what happens to the irrational movement of the stars? Why do some revere chance, and others spontaneity? Why do they think that everything is carried along at random and haphazardly? Is it because of those who live decently and moderately, or because of the men you said hold society together, whom I have shown to be the common plague of the world? Clearly it is because of the latter. No one is indignant because so-and-so lives as a philosopher, or because he is decent, moderate and self-controlled and looks down on the things of this life. They are indignant because so-and-so is rich, lives in luxury, grasps and plunders, and because though he is wicked and full of countless vices, he is illustrious and prospers. These are the charges and complaints of those who do not believe in God. These are the things the many stumble over. As for those who live decently, not only would they never utter any of these words; they would even condemn themselves for anything that led them to accuse God's providence. If everyone, or even most people, chose to live this way, no one would have thought of saying these things. Nor would the crowning evil of all have come in, the question of where evils come from. For if evils did not exist or appear, who would have been led to search for the cause of evils, and who would have caused countless heresies to spring up from this search? Marcion, Mani, Valentinus and most of the pagans took their starting point from here. But if everyone lived as a philosopher, there would be no room for these questions. Even if from nowhere else, at least from this excellent way of life everyone would have learned that we live under God as our King, and that he governs and steers our affairs according to his wisdom and understanding. His providence is at work even now, but it is not easily seen because of the thick fog these men have spread over the whole world. If it were not for this, God's providence would shine clearly for all to see, as at the steady light of noon in a bright calm. Suppose there were no courts, no accusers, no informers, no tortures or punishments, no prisons or penalties, no confiscations or fines, no fears or dangers, no enmities, no plots, no slanders or hatred, no famines or plagues, nor any of the other evils I have listed, but all lived with fitting decency. Who among all the living would have disputed God's providence? No one. As it is, the same thing happens as when a storm comes on: the helmsman does his work and saves the ship, but the passengers do not see the precision of his skill because of their confusion and fear and their anguish over the dangers hanging over them. In the same way, God steers this universe even now, but most people do not see it because of the storm and turmoil in human affairs, which these men above all produce. So they not only overturn society but also damage true religion. One would not be wrong to call them common enemies. They live in opposition to the salvation of others, and by foul doctrines and impure lives they sink those who sail with them.

[?] …I would not have praised those who drive them away, but would have turned away from them as common enemies of society. For by hiding the lamps and taking the lights from the city out into the desert, they would be robbing those who live inside the city of the greatest goods. But if there is no one who will promise this, what is the use of sending boys to teachers? There they will learn vice before they learn letters, and in seeking to gain the lesser thing they will lose the greater: the whole strength and health of the soul. “What then?” he says. “Shall we tear down the schools?” That is not what I am saying. I am saying that we must not demolish the building of virtue and bury the soul alive. If the soul is sound, no harm will come from a lack of skill in speaking. But if it is corrupted, the damage is enormous, even if the tongue happens to be very sharp. Indeed the damage is all the greater, the more of that power there is. For when wickedness acquires skill in speaking, it does far worse harm than ignorance does. “But what if they go there,” he says, “and besides having a slower tongue, they also fall away from that virtue?” And what if, tell me, they stay here, and besides corrupting their souls, gain nothing from school toward eloquence? I have more right to say this than you have to say that. Why so? Because even if the future of either course is uncertain, yours is more uncertain. How, and why? Because the pursuit of eloquence requires good character, but good character does not require the addition of eloquence. Self-control can be achieved even without this education, but no one could ever acquire the power of speech without good morals, since all his time would be spent on vice and debauchery. So what you fear there, you must fear here too, and much more here, since failures here are more frequent and the danger concerns greater things. There one needs to work at only one thing, but here two must be mastered, since one cannot be had without the other: one cannot learn letters without self-control. And if you like, let us suppose that the impossible is possible. What good would skill in these things do us if we are wounded in our vital parts? And what harm would come from lacking it, if we succeed in the greatest things? This is agreed not only by us, who laugh at pagan wisdom and consider it foolishness, but even by the pagan philosophers themselves. That is why most of them did not care much about the matter. Some even despised it completely and remained unlearned; they spent their whole lives on the ethical part of philosophy, shone brilliantly and became famous. Anacharsis, Crates and Diogenes made no effort over this, and some say that neither did Socrates. The man who excelled all others in this art, and who knew Socrates' affairs more precisely than anyone else, would bear us witness. Once, bringing Socrates into court to make his defense, he made him say to the judges in his defense speech: “From me you will hear the whole truth, not, however, [?]

…to shape his soul. I went up to this tutor (for he happened to be one of those who live in the mountains) and tried to learn why, when he had taken hold of such wisdom, he had lowered himself to the life of a tutor. He said that only a little time remained for him in this work, and told us the whole story from the beginning. "This child," he said, "has a father who is harsh and rough and excited about worldly affairs, but a mother who is moderate, chaste and gentle, and looks to heaven alone. Now the father, since he has won many successes in war, wants to bring his son into his father's rank. The mother neither wishes nor desires this, but even strongly [?], and she prays and longs to see him illustrious in the monastic way of life. But she did not dare say this to the father. She feared that he might suspect this very thing and bind the boy before his time with the ropes of worldly life, draw him away from this zeal, lead him to the soldier's belt and all the slackness that comes with it, and make it impossible for him to be set right afterward. So she devised another stratagem. She called me to her house, shared all this with me, took the child's right hand and placed it in my hands. When I asked why she was doing this, she said that only one stratagem remained to us for the boy's salvation: that I should be willing to take the child and bear to come here in the role of a tutor. She would persuade the father that an education in letters would be useful to him even if he chose the military life. 'If I can bring this about,' she said, 'you will have him to yourself from then on in a foreign place, with neither his father nor anyone of the household troubling you, and you will be able to shape him with complete freedom and make him live as if he were spending his days in a monastery. So consent, and promise to play out this drama with me. My concern is not about trifles. The struggle and the danger are for the soul of my child. Do not stand by while the one dearest of all to me is in danger, but snatch him now from the snares that surround him on every side, from the storm, from the surge.
