If you will not grant me this favor, I now call God as witness between us, and I testify that I have left undone nothing that bears on the salvation of his soul, and that I am innocent of this child's blood. If it should happen that he comes to some harm, as is likely for one who is young and lives in such luxury and slackness, then on that day God will require this child's soul from you and from your hands.' Adding these words and more besides, and weeping violently and piteously, she persuaded me to undertake this task, and sent me off with these instructions." And her stratagem did not prove vain. That noble man trained the boy so well in a short time, and kindled in him so great a fire of this desire, that he threw everything away at once and ran off to the desert, and in turn needed another bridle that could turn him back from that excessive asceticism to a moderate one. For there was a fear that by this zeal he might reveal the drama before its time and stir up a hard war against his mother, his tutor and the monks everywhere. If the father had learned of this flight, he would not have stopped at anything to drive out those holy men, not only those who had received the boy but all the others as well. So I took this boy, and after saying these things and more besides, [?] [Apparatus, partly illegible: two manuscripts read ὑποισχησόμενος [?]; Savile and Morel ὑποστησόμενος; Savile and another read τὸν οὐδὲ ἑαυτῷ. Below, Morel reads ἐκόλασε, others κολάσω.]

…it would be cruelty to let a man who cannot even defend himself, but lies there taking countless wounds and making the others weaker, be cut to pieces in the thick of the fight, when he ought to be dragged out of the battle. One would punish a general in the same way if he withdrew from the battle line those able to fight, and ordered the wounded and fallen, who throw the rest into confusion, to lie in the midst of it forever. 13. But many fathers each insist on this, wanting to see their son living a life of letters, as though they knew for certain that he will reach the goal of learning. Let us not argue about this, and let us not say that he will fail. For the sake of argument, let us grant that he will certainly succeed in his efforts and reach the summit. Now let a twofold choice be set before us: if he goes to the schools, let his contest be for learning; if he goes to the deserts, let it be for his soul. Tell me, where is it better for him to win? If he succeeds in both, I wish it too; but if one must be lacking, it is better to choose the better. "Yes," he says, "but how can we be sure of this very thing, that he will stand firm and persevere and not fall away? Many have fallen." And how can you be sure that he will not stand firm and persevere? Many have stood firm, more than those who have fallen, so that we ought to take courage from them rather than be afraid because of the others. And why do you not fear this very thing in the case of letters, where you ought to fear it most? Among the monks, few out of many have failed; but in the study of letters, few out of many have succeeded. And not for this reason alone, but for many others too, one might reasonably fear that path more. A child's lack of talent, the teachers' ignorance, the tutors' negligence, the father's lack of leisure, a shortage of money for expenses and fees, differences of character, the wickedness, envy and spite of fellow students, and many other things ruin the outcome. And not only these, but after he has got through them there are more. For when he has overcome everything and reached the very summit of education, tripped up by none of these, another ambush lies in wait for him there. The hostility of a ruler, the envy of rivals in the same profession, hard times, the lack of friends and poverty have often cut men off from the goal. It is not so with the monks. Only one thing is needed, a noble and good eagerness; and if this is present, nothing prevents a man from reaching the goal of virtue. How then is it not unjust to despair and tremble where the good hopes are clear and close at hand, but not to despair where the prospects of the other path are more remote and cut short by so many hindrances, and to be confident where the difficulties are plainer and more numerous? To look, in the case of letters, not at the painful things that often happen but at the good things that rarely turn out, and to do the opposite in the case of the monks: where the hopes of good are many, to incline toward the painful things alone, and where the hopes of the contrary [are many], the good [?] [Apparatus, garbled: Savile and one manuscript read διαμαρτήσεται; Morel and another διαμαρτήσετε. After διδασκαλεῖα one manuscript adds διδασκάλους [?] … φοιτῆς; … ψυχῆς ἐχέτω τὸν ἀγῶνα· εἰς δὲ ἐρημίας ὑπὲρ τῆς … two manuscripts read ἔνθα δὲ τὰ μακρότερα ὑπὸ τοσούτων δὲ τῶν δυσχερῶν ἀνακοπτόμενα κωλυμάτων [?]; τὰ δὲ τῶν δυσχερῶν σαφέστερα [?]. Genesis 47 [?].]

…evils. It gives no name of layman or of monk; this distinction was introduced by human thinking. The Scriptures know nothing of these things, but want everyone to live the life of monks, even those who happen to have wives. Listen, at any rate, to what Paul says—and when I say Paul, I mean Christ again. Writing to men who have wives and are raising children, he demands of them all the strictness that befits monks. Cutting away all luxury, both in clothing and in food, he writes these words: "Women should adorn themselves in modest apparel, with reverence and self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly clothing." And again: "She who lives in self-indulgence is dead while she lives." And again: "If we have food and clothing, with these we shall be content." What more than this could anyone demand of monks? Again, when he teaches others to control the tongue, he lays down strict laws, such as even monks find it hard to fulfill. He does away not only with obscenity and foolish talk but also with jesting. He cuts away from the mouth of the faithful not only wrath and anger and bitterness but also shouting: "Let all wrath and anger and shouting and slander be put away from you, with all malice." Do these seem small things to you? Then wait, and you will hear things far greater than these, which he commands everyone concerning forbearance: "Do not let the sun go down on your anger." "See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for all." And again: "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Do you see how intense a philosophy and patience this is, climbing to the very peak? Hear also how much he commands about love, the chief of all goods. By exalting it and describing its achievements, he showed that he demands of laymen the same love that Christ demanded of the disciples. For as the Savior said that the ultimate limit of love is to lay down one's life for one's friends, so Paul hinted at the same thing when he said, "Love does not seek its own," and he commands us to pursue love of this kind. So even if this alone had been said, it would be sufficient proof that laymen are required to do the same things as monks, for love is the bond and the root of much virtue. But as it is, he also sets it out point by point. What greater philosophy than this could anyone seek? When he commands us to rise above anger, wrath, shouting, the desire for money, the belly, extravagance, vainglory and all other worldly things, and to have nothing in common with the earth; when he orders us to put our members to death, it is clear that he demands of us the same strictness that Christ demanded of the disciples, and wants us to be as dead to sin as those who have already died and been buried. This is why he says, "For whoever has died has been justified from sin." And there are places where by his exhortation he leads us to imitate Christ, and not only the disciples. When he urges us to love, he draws his examples from there; and likewise when he urges us not to bear grudges, and to be humble. So when he addresses not only monks, nor only the disciples, but also… [Apparatus: two manuscripts and Morel read ἀποδώσει; Savile ἀποδῷ. Two manuscripts read "to walk the narrow way."]

…"concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord." That the layman and the monk must reach the same peak, and that both will receive the same wounds if they fall, I think not even the most contentious and shameless person will dispute any longer. 15. Now that this has been clearly shown, come, let us examine this point as well: which of them will fall more easily and readily? Or perhaps here we do not even need an examination. The man who has a wife will easily achieve chastity, since he enjoys great consolation; in the other matters this advantage is not much in evidence. Yet even here we would see more married men falling than monks. Not as many leave the monasteries for marriage as rise from their wives' beds to go to prostitutes. And if they fall so badly where the struggle is easy for them, what will they do with the other passions, in which they are troubled more than monks? Desire assails the monks more strongly, since they have no contact with women; but the other passions cannot even come near the monks, while they drive the laymen with all their force and push them headlong. And if, where the war blows most fiercely, the monks prevail more than those who do not suffer it, it is clear that they will stand far more easily than the laymen in the other passions, by which they are not troubled. For love of money, and the desire for luxury and power and all the rest, are naturally overcome more easily by monks than by laymen. In a battle we would say that the lighter part of the fighting is not where the dead fall one after another in heaps, but where they fall few and far between; and we must judge these matters the same way. It is not the man who moves about in the thick of things but the man who sits in the mountains who will more easily overcome greed. The former will be caught easily, and once caught by greed he must be counted among idolaters. As for his relatives, the monk will not choose to neglect them if he has money, but will readily give them everything; whereas the other will not only neglect them but will wrong strangers no less, and this again is another form of idolatry, worse than the first. And why mention all the rest, which monks fight off easily but which throw down laymen with great violence? How then do you not fear or tremble at leading your son into this life, where he will quickly be caught by vice? Or does idolatry seem a small thing to you, and being worse than unbelievers, and renouncing the service of God by one's deeds—all of which those bound to worldly life will suffer more easily than monks? Do you see that the fear is a pretext? If one must fear, it should not be for those fleeing the waves, nor for those hastening to the harbor, but for those tossed about in the storm and the tempest. Shipwrecks happen more quickly there, because the troubles are greater and those who must stand against them are more careless. Here the waves are not so many, the calm is great, and those who will fight against them are more zealous. This is why we too draw them to the desert: not merely so that they may put on sackcloth, nor so that they may put on iron collars, [Apparatus, garbled: others read τουτέστι [?] … others τρυφῆς. The Camaldolese manuscript reads υἱόν. The words "nor for those hastening to the harbor" are missing in [?].]

…I would say this to them: first, it is uncertain whether children will follow from marriage at all; second, even when they come, the distress is greater. We do not reap as much joy from them as we do grief from the daily care, the anxiety and the fears on their account. "And to whom," he says, "shall we leave our fields and houses and slaves and gold?" For I hear them lamenting this too. To the one who was to inherit them before all this, and now so much more than before, since he will now be a safer guardian and master of them. Back then, many things threatened them: moths, the long passage of time, robbers, informers, the envious, the uncertainty of the future, the changeableness of human affairs, and finally death would have deprived the son both of the money and of these possessions. But now he has stored his wealth above all these things, having found an inviolable place, where none of the things I have mentioned may set foot. Heaven is such a place: no plot can reach it, it is more fertile than any land, and it lets those who have deposited riches there reap their fruits in great abundance. So this is not the time to say such things. If the child had been going to be a layman, then you should have lamented and said: "To whom shall we leave the fields, to whom the gold, to whom the rest of these things?"

For now his mastery is so abundant that not even after his departure from here does he lose his ownership of them; rather, he enjoys their profit most of all when we depart from here. And if you want to see him master in this life too, one would see this happening to the monk rather than to the layman. Tell me, who is more truly master: the one who spends and gives with complete freedom, or the one who out of stinginess does not even dare to touch his money, but buries it and keeps his hands off his own goods as if they belonged to someone else? The one who spends uselessly and at random, or the one who spends as he ought? The one who sows the earth, or the one who does this work in heaven? The one who is not permitted to give all his own goods to whomever he wishes, or the one who is free of all those who demand such contributions? Many press upon the farmer and the merchant from every side, forcing them to pay taxes, each demanding his own share. But no one anywhere will appear with such threats against the man who wants to spend on the needy, so here too he is more truly master. Or if a man spends on prostitutes, on his belly, on parasites and flatterers, disgraces his reputation, ruins his salvation and becomes a laughingstock, you say he is master of what he spends; but if he spends it with great wisdom on true glory and benefit and on what pleases God, is he no longer master? Then you are acting as if, seeing someone throw his goods into the sewers, you said he was master of them, but when he used them for necessary purposes, you lamented as though he had no authority over what he spent. Or rather, such people should be compared not to those who simply spend, but to those who spend to the ruin of their own heads. For those expenditures more splendidly, abundantly and securely… [Apparatus: one manuscript reads τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων, others τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Below, two manuscripts read πλοῦτον ἀνέθετο, the editions ἀπέθετο. … ταῦτα [?]. Others read πολλαχόθεν ἐπιστήσονται. Two manuscripts read τοὺς υἱοὺς παραβάλλων.]

…and because of the corruption all around, you drag these boys into the thick of it as if they had already succeeded and grown strong, [?] those who are about to learn [?] to make the house inaccessible [?]; you do not let them go off and be trained in the desert, [?] to dine and sleep in a teacher's house [?]. It is as if someone ordered the man who could set up countless trophies to practice warfare at his leisure, but laid down a law that the inexperienced man, who cannot so much as peep at a battle, must for that very reason move about in the thick of the fighting, as though the task were hard to accomplish, and so placed greater hindrances in his way. Besides this, one must also know that after marriage a man cannot be his own master, but one of two things is unavoidable: either he must always have relations with his wife whenever she wishes, or, if he withdraws because he wishes to practice continence, he is charged with adultery. Why speak of the other constraints, those of children, and the cares of the household, which can blunt all eagerness and spread a heavy numbness over the soul? 18. Therefore it is better to arm him from his earliest youth, while he is his own master and free, not only for the reasons already given but no less for the one I am about to give. The man who takes up this philosophy near the end of his life spends all his time trying to wash away the sins committed in his earlier years, and all his effort is used up on this; and often even so it is not enough, but he departs still bearing traces of his wounds. But the one who stripped for the contest from his earliest youth does not spend his time on this, nor sit tending his wounds, but takes the prizes from the very start. The former is glad if he can make up for all his defeats, but the latter sets up trophies from the very starting line and adds victory to victory. Like an Olympic victor who goes from earliest youth to old age from one proclamation to the next, he departs to that world with his head crowned with countless garlands. Among which, then, do you want your son to be: among those who through their great boldness can look even the archangels in the face, or among those who stand with everyone else and keep the last rank? For they will certainly receive the last rank, and even that only if they manage to get past all the hindrances I have just listed: if an untimely death does not snatch them away first, if they are not hindered later by a wife, if they do not receive so many wounds that the time of old age is not enough to heal them, and if they keep their resolve firm and unshaken to the end. Only when all these things come together will they barely be ranked among the last. Do you want your son to be among these, or among those who shine at the front of the battle line? "And who is so wretched," he says, "as to pray for those things rather than these for his children? But we want their company; we want them to be with us." I want this too, and I pray no less than you who begot them that they may return to their father's house and repay you for their upbringing, with a recompense such as they could not find anywhere else. But let us not demand this of them now. For how is it not absurd that, when sending them away for letters, you banish them from their homeland for a long time… [Apparatus, garbled: [?] διαδράναι ἅπερ; "and city and nations" [?]. Others read λυμήνασθαι. Below, two manuscripts read οὐ μόνον τοῖς πρός; in the same place, some read παντὸς ἐπιτεύξασθαι.]

…shall we delight in our beloved children only; we ourselves too will return home having reaped the greatest benefits, and often we will even stay with them, captured by the love of philosophy. So let us call them back then, when they have grown strong and are able to benefit others; only then let us draw them out, so that the light may be shared by all, so that the lamp may be set on the lampstand. Then you will see what children you are fathers of, and what children those whom you count blessed are fathers of. Then you will know the gains of philosophy: when they heal people sick with incurable diseases, when they are proclaimed common benefactors and protectors and saviours, when they go about like angels among people on earth, when everyone looks to them. Or rather, whatever we may say is nothing compared with what can be seen in actual experience and in the facts themselves. This is what lawgivers too ought to have done, if anything were being done as it should be: not to brandish terrors over the young once they have become men, but to train and mould them while they are still children. Then there would have been no need of the threats that come later. As it is, what happens is as if a physician told a patient nothing while he was ill, and did not show him the means by which he might be rid of his disease, but then, once he was ruined and past cure, laid down countless rules for him. For the lawgivers, too, take us in hand to instruct us only once we have been perverted. But Paul does not do so. From the beginning, from earliest youth, he sets teachers of virtue over them, preventing vice from getting in. For this is the best teaching: not to let wickedness first gain the upper hand and afterwards look for a way to drive it out, but to do and strive for everything so that our nature may become inaccessible to it. Therefore I urge you not only not to hinder others who wish to do this, but to lend a hand yourselves, to save the ship and get it ready to sail with a fair wind. For if we had all adopted this view, and led them to virtue before everything else, treating this as our real task and everything else as secondary, the blessings would be so great that if I described them now I would seem to be boasting. But if anyone wishes to learn, he will come to know it well from the deeds themselves. He will owe us much gratitude, and still more, before us, to God, when he sees the heavenly way of life springing up on earth, and the teachings about the good things to come and about the resurrection already confirmed from this, even among the unbelievers themselves.

19. That this is no empty boast is clear from the following. When we speak to them of the way of life of those who live in the deserts, they have nothing to say against it, but they think they make a strong case, and argue contentiously, from the small number of those who succeed. But if we had planted this fruit in the cities, and good order had gained the force of law and rule, and we were training our children before all else to be friends of God, and were teaching them spiritual lessons instead of the others and before all the others, all troubles would have fled away, the present life would have been rid of countless evils, and what is said of the life to come, that pain and sorrow and [sighing] have fled away…

[Textual notes:] Two manuscripts: αὐτούς ("them"). Savile in the margin: "that the light be set". [?] "we shall say nothing such as". "we were training". "all troubles would have fled away".

…in so great a crowd the victory will come down to one man, they still toil and endure hardship. And yet there is no comparison between that contest and this one, not only because of the outcome of the contests, but because there only one can go away crowned. Here, superiority and inferiority do not lie in one man departing uncrowned and another crowned, but in one receiving a more glorious proclamation and another a lesser one, while all still receive one. In short, if we were willing to mould our children from the beginning and to hand them over to those who wish to train them, it would not be unlikely that they would stand in the front rank of the army. For God would not have overlooked such eagerness and zeal. He would have lent his own hand and touched the statue, and when that hand is at work, nothing that is being made can possibly fail. Or rather, it cannot fail to reach the height of splendour and glory, provided only that our own part follows. For if women were able to persuade God to join them in caring for their children, much more shall we be able to do this, if we wish. So as not to make my speech long, I will pass over the others, though I could mention many, and will recall only one.

20. There was a Jewish woman named Hannah. This Hannah bore one child, and did not expect to bear another, for she had obtained even this one with difficulty and with many tears, since she was barren. Though she saw her rival often trampling on her because of this, even so she felt nothing like what you feel. When she had that son, she let him stay with her only as long as he needed to be nursed. When he no longer needed this nourishment, she took him and at once dedicated him to God, and did not ask him ever again to set foot in his father's house; he lived continually in the temple of God. And if ever she longed to see him, as a mother would, she did not call the child to her, but went up to him herself with his father, keeping her hands off him from then on as an offering consecrated to God. And that young man became so noble and great that, when God had turned away from the Hebrew race because of the wickedness that had flooded it, and no longer gave them oracles or showed them any vision, he drew him back again by his virtue. He persuaded him to grant the same favours as before, and called back prophecy, which had flown away. And he accomplished this not when he had come of age, but while he was still a little child. For there was, it says, no distinct vision, and the word was precious. Yet even though things were like this, God continually gave oracles through him. So great is the gain of always yielding our own possessions to him, and of giving up everything: not only money or possessions, but even our very children. For if we are commanded to do this with our own soul, how much more with everything else. The patriarch Abraham did this too, or rather something much greater, and that is why he received his son back with greater glory. For it is then that we most truly have our children, when we hand them over to the Master. He will protect them far better than we can, since he also cares for them far more. Do you not see, in households too, of the…

[Textual notes:] Morel and one manuscript: παραστήσεται; others: περιστήσεται. [?] συνεφάψεσθαι. Morel's edition: πρὸς ἑαυτήν; Savile: παρ’ ἑαυτήν; two manuscripts: παρ’ [?].

…let us act so as to leave them the wealth of piety, which lasts and travels on with them, and can benefit them greatly not only here but there as well. Worldly wealth will not go with us. Even here it perishes first, and often destroys its owners along with it. But this wealth will be secure both here and there, and will keep those who possess it in great safety. For this is how things stand: whoever prefers earthly things to spiritual ones will lose both, but whoever desires heavenly things will certainly obtain earthly ones too. These are not my words, but the words of the Lord himself, who will provide these things. For seek, he says, the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. What could equal this honour? Take care of spiritual things, he says, and leave all that is yours to me. Just as an affectionate father who takes charge of the care of the house, the management of the servants and everything else might urge his son to devote himself to philosophy alone, so too does God. Let us then obey, and seek the kingdom of God. Then we shall see our children approved everywhere, we ourselves shall be illustrious with them, and we shall enjoy the good things of the present, if only we love those that are to come and are heavenly. If you obey these words, they will bring you a great reward; but if you contradict and disobey them, a harsher punishment. For you cannot take refuge in excuses, or say that there was no one teaching these things. Indeed, even before our words this excuse had been taken away, since nature has an exact standard for judging what is good and what is not, this philosophy is set before us everywhere, and the evils of this life are enough to drive even those who passionately love it into the desert. So even if we had kept silent, as I said, the excuse would have been taken away; and now much more so, after these long discourses and so much exhortation, both that drawn from the facts and the clearer one drawn from the divine Scriptures. And even if it were possible for those who stay at home not to be utterly corrupted, but at least to attain the lowest rank of salvation, we would still hardly escape punishment, for hindering those eager to walk a stricter life, and for holding back in worldly affairs those eager to fly to heaven. But when not even this is possible, when they must certainly perish and the danger concerns the ultimate things, what pardon shall we have, what defence? We draw upon ourselves the reckoning not only for our own sins but, more severely, for those the children commit afterwards. For I do not think they will be punished as severely for whatever they stumble into later, once dragged down into this storm, as you will be, who imposed this necessity on them. For if it is better for one who causes a single person to stumble to be drowned in the sea with a millstone, what punishment and penalty will be enough for those who show such cruelty and harshness toward their children? Therefore I beg you to give up your contentiousness and to become fathers of children who live the life of philosophy. For you cannot say what I hear many putting forward as a pretext: "But what is this…"
